name: Spades (Standard)
description: Spades is a trick-taking card game devised in the United States in the 1930s. It is played by four players in partnerships, using a standard 52-card deck. Spades are always the trump suit. The object is to score points by winning at least the number of tricks bid in each hand. Bids are made before play begins. 'Bags' (overtricks) and 'Nil' bids add strategic depth.

overview.description: Spades is a trick-taking card game devised in the United States in the 1930s. It is played by four players in partnerships, using a standard 52-card deck. history.origins: Developed in Cincinnati, Ohio, or Indiana in the late 1930s. Became popular among college students.
timeline: 1990s: Very popular online (MSN Zone, Yahoo Games).
Present: A staple in Black American culture and tournaments.
history.cultural: Known for 'talking across the board' (trash talk) and complex signaling.
history.evolution: The introduction of the 'Nil' bid transformed it from a simple Whist variant into a high-stakes game.

setup.deck: Standard 52-card French deck. Spades may also be played with one or two Jokers or with predetermined cards removed; with six or more players a second deck is often used.

rules.objective: To score points, generally 500. Points are accrued by winning at least the number of tricks bid in each hand; they are lost by failing to take at least that many, or in some cases by taking too many (bags).
rules.gameplay: Deal 13 cards each. Each player bids 0–13 tricks (Nil = 0). Player to dealer's left leads first; may not lead a spade until spades are broken or holder has only spades. Must follow suit if able; otherwise may play any card. Trick won by highest spade if any, else highest of led suit. Winner leads next. Thirteen tricks per hand. Score 10 per bid trick if made; 1 per overtrick (bag); 10 bags = -100. Nil: +100 or -100; blind nil: ±200. First to 500 wins.
keyRules: Spades are always trump. Must follow suit if able. Spades may not be led until broken or only spades in hand. Partnership bids are summed; team must make combined bid. Overtricks (bags) score 1 each; 10 bags cost 100 points.

strategy.basic: Count your winners (Aces/Kings). Count your trumps. If you have 5 trumps, you can usually win 3-4 tricks. Don't overbid on Queens unless you hold the King/Ace.
strategy.intermediate: Covering a Nil: If your partner bids Nil, your job is to take every trick they might accidentally win. Lead low to them so they can duck. Trump if necessary to save them.
strategy.advanced: Bag Management: If you are way ahead, take bags to force opponents to react. If you are close to 10 bags (-100), try to duck tricks or let opponents win cheap ones.
tips: Don't lead a singleton King unless desperate.
Aces usually win the first round of a suit.

variations.name: Blind Nil
variations.description: Nil bid declared before looking at cards; may exchange two cards with partner after bids. Scores ±200. Often allowed only when team is 100+ points behind.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Variation only changes bidding and scoring rules; no engine constant overrides needed.

variations.name: 10-for-200
variations.description: Bid of 10 tricks: score 200 if exactly 10 (or at least 10) tricks taken; lose 200 otherwise. Also called wheels.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Variation only changes scoring for 10-trick bid; no engine constant overrides needed.

variations.name: Partnership Bidding
variations.description: Partners discuss and agree a single team bid instead of bidding in turn. Minimum bid often 4. No Nil in some house rules.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Variation only changes bidding procedure; no engine constant overrides needed.

scoring.description: 10 points per bid trick. 1 point for each overtrick (Bag). 10 Bags = -100 penalty. Nil: ±100; blind nil: ±200. First to 500 wins.
scoring.winCondition: Meet your bid. Avoid bags if possible. First team to 500 points wins.
